## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.todaymeta}
Session 3 of day 3, on the slope of the claim as a posterior distribution
:::

:::: {.todaybox}
::: {.nonincremental .fs-85}
1. Priors – the posterior of the two-way slope, and what its priors imply before the data enter
2. Partial pooling – a slope for each country, each estimated partly from the others
3. Few clusters – errors that persist within a country, and the slope across the models
4. The checks – the computation, the posterior predictive check and the sensitivity to the priors
:::
::::

::: {.todaytake .fs-85}
You leave able to read a posterior distribution, to say what its priors imply, and to judge what a Bayesian model adds when 27 countries carry the evidence
:::

::: {.todaymeta}
The models were fitted once, with brms; you work in the workspace, in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.)
:::

::: notes
The third session goes back to the panel and estimates the slope of the claim by Bayesian methods. Nothing about the data changes, but the slope becomes a distribution, about which we can make direct statements of probability, and the dependence of the years of a country, which the CR2 test repairs after the fit, has to be written into the model itself. We start with the priors, which a Bayesian model needs for every parameter, and with what they imply before the data enter. Then partial pooling, which gives every country a slope of its own, each estimated partly from the others. Then the problem of few clusters, taken up from the Bayesian side, and last the checks that a Bayesian workflow runs before anyone reads a posterior. The models take a while to fit, so they were fitted once, and the slides read their results.
:::
